layout.description: Is willpower a battery that runs down? In 1998, students who had to eat radishes instead of chocolate gave up on an unsolvable puzzle after about eight instead of almost nineteen minutes. Two large preregistered replications with 2,141 and 3,531 people found almost no effect. Original, replication, limits and state of research.
layout.companion_text: Gritwerk retells published experiments: setup, measure, result, limits, replication status. Not run by us.

beats.spoken: Is willpower a battery that runs down? A famous experiment from nineteen ninety-eight seemed to show it. Then came replications with thousands.

data.question: Is willpower a battery?
data.cite: Baumeister et al. 1998 · J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 74(5) · p. 1254

beats.spoken: Here is the original. Sixty-seven hungry students came to a lab that smelled of fresh cookies. One group could eat chocolate, another only radishes, a third got nothing. Then came an unsolvable puzzle. The measure: how long they kept going.

data.headline: The original
data.cite: Baumeister et al. 1998 · J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 74(5) · p. 1254 f.

beats.spoken: Those who had to eat radishes gave up after about eight minutes. With chocolate it was almost nineteen. That is where the battery idea came from.

data.headline: Result 1998
data.cite: Baumeister et al. 1998 · J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 74(5) · p. 1255

beats.spoken: Earlier studies combined showed an effect of zero point six two. In twenty sixteen, twenty-three labs tested the idea with over two thousand people, though with a computer task. Result: zero point zero four. In twenty twenty-one, with puzzles like the original: zero point zero six.

data.headline: Original vs replication
data.cite: Hagger et al. 2016, p. 554 f. · Vohs et al. 2021, manuscript p. 18

beats.spoken: The limits: different tasks, mostly students, short lab tests. Self-control still matters. But the empty battery picture does not hold up.

limits.text: short lab tests, not daily life

evidence.cite: Hagger et al., Perspect. Psychol. Sci.

data.cite: Hagger et al. 2016 · Vohs et al. 2021

beats.spoken: Your test: for five working days, write down the one task of the day before you open anything else. In the evening, one box if it got done. It proves nothing, but you will see how often it works. More real experiments: follow Gritwerk.
